strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-identified limitation of spectral feature learning for NPIV (outcome-agnostic features, following Meunier et al. [27]), and the core idea is clean: augmenting the contrastive loss is shown rigorously (Proposition 1, proof in B.1) to be equivalent to learning a truncated SVD of an augmented operator T_δ.

The theoretical treatment is careful and largely self-contained: the perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-Θ, Weyl, Eckart-Young) used to relate singular subspaces of T_δ to those of T (Propositions 4-8, Theorem 4) is a real technical contribution, and the 'good'/'bad' scenario corollaries give concrete insight into when one feature can replace k spurious ones.
Theorem 1 provides a non-asymptotic, high-probability 2SLS bound that improves on prior in-expectation guarantees, with assumptions that are standard for this literature.

Experiments are reasonably well designed: a controlled synthetic setting where misalignment can be tuned, a new and better-motivated 'hard' dSprites structural function (h_new) whose spectral misalignment is empirically verified (Fig. 5), and an OPE application with complete protocol details (hyperparameter grids, seeds, architectures in Tables 1-5), which supports reproducibility.

The discussion of limitations is unusually honest: the authors explicitly acknowledge that the optimality gap E_d is not bounded, that δ selection via the stage-2 loss lacks consistency guarantees (Section D.8 even argues 2SLS-loss model selection is generally unprincipled), and that higher-rank perturbations are unresolved.
weaknesses: The end-to-end theory is incomplete: the final error bounds all depend on the optimality gap E_d(θ, ω, δ), which the authors concede is unbounded ('an open problem in its own right'). Consequently, Theorem 4 and the 'bad scenario' result do not provide a fully supported statistical guarantee for the method as implemented — the central claim of a 'full generalization error bound' (Contribution 2) overstates what is proven.

The key hyperparameter δ lacks theoretical or reliable automatic selection. The recommended procedure is an ad hoc heuristic (Section 6.4), performance is explicitly 'contingent on the choice of δ', and the alternative (stage-2 loss tuning) is, by the authors' own admission in D.8, unprincipled. This significantly weakens practical usability of the method.

The empirical case in the hardest setting is not decisive: on OPE, AugSpecIV performs well on Cartpole but poorly on Mountain Car, and the paper concedes 'no OPE method performed uniformly well'; the dSprites results for δ up to 1.0 actually show degradation relative to δ=0.3-0.5, and boxplots are based on only 9 fitted models.

The 'bad scenario' bound (Eq. 18) has awkward prefactors (e.g., a term scaling with 5∥h0∥/λ_k²·(∥s1∥/∥s1∥) that is not informative as written) and requires a strong signal-to-noise condition ∥s1∥ ≫ λ_k^{-2}∥q1∥, so its practical reach is limited.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a one-parameter regularization added to the existing SpecIV contrastive loss, and the perturbation machinery (Wedin, Weyl) is standard; the contribution is best viewed as an increment on Meunier et al. [27] rather than a new framework.

Notation in Section 4 and Appendix B is dense and occasionally inconsistent (e.g., overloading of bars/underbars in the partition decomposition, 'call' vs 'called' in Theorem 5), which impedes verification of the proofs; some steps in Propositions 6-7 would benefit from more careful justification.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: outcome-awareness in spectral feature learning for NPIV is achieved by a rank-one augmentation of the conditional expectation operator T with the outcome regression r0, turning the modified contrastive loss into a best rank-d approximation of the augmented operator T_delta (Prop. 4.1). This gives a clean operator-theoretic bridge from the loss to downstream guarantees.

The theoretical analysis is substantive: a high-probability, representation-agnostic 2SLS excess-risk bound (Thm 5.1), a careful perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-Theta plus Weyl) that relates the singular subspaces of T_delta back to those of T (Thm C.6, Props C.1-C.5), and explicit 'good'/'bad' scenario corollaries showing that the outcome-aware method can recover a structural function aligned with a low singular function of T using d=1 features while standard SpecIV would need d>=k. The excess-loss-to-operator-gap bound (Prop A.4) is stated to be new even for delta=0, which is a genuine standalone contribution.

Experiments are thoughtfully designed and honest: a controlled synthetic setting where alignment and spectral decay are parameterized, a new, harder dSprites structural function (h_new, rotation-based) with empirical verification of the spectral misalignment diagnosis, and an OPE experiment where dynamic spectral misalignment naturally arises. The appendix includes an extensive naive outcome-aware baseline study, post-hoc rejection analysis, and rank-K perturbation preliminaries, which strengthen the credibility of the empirical claims.

Limitations are discussed candidly: the guarantees are explicitly conditioned on successful representation learning (small population optimality gap), the theoretical justification for second-stage-loss model selection is shown to be lacking (Sec E.8), and the authors clearly flag that driving Delta_delta to zero by DNN training is left open.

The comparison to the closely related Bruns-Smith (2025) work is fair and specific, distinguishing the method by requiring the Z-features to also be useful for the IV problem without post-hoc testing, and requiring weaker restrictions on ill-posedness for strong-norm convergence.
weaknesses: The main statistical guarantees are conditional: they control downstream 2SLS error given a small population optimality gap E_d of the learned features, but the paper provides no optimization or generalization theory for actually achieving small E_d with neural networks (acknowledged as open). The end-to-end story thus relies on empirical performance rather than a complete guarantee.

Delta selection remains partly heuristic. The three proposed procedures (estimated alignment, loss-balance heuristic, second-stage loss) are practical but lack consistency guarantees; notably, the theory-aware alignment estimator A(delta) becomes unstable precisely when delta grows large (||omega||->1), which is the regime where the 'bad scenario' guarantees apply. The chosen 5%-relative-improvement rule is ad hoc.
The code repository link appears to be blank in the manuscript ('can be found at .'), which is a reproducibility concern for the reproduction of figures.

Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow: DFIV, KIV and vanilla SpecIV are included, but there is no direct empirical comparison against the most closely related adaptive method (Bruns-Smith, 2025) beyond conceptual discussion; the appendix baseline is an in-house variant rather than that published method.

Some parts of the theory follow fairly directly from standard tools (Wedin sin-Theta, Weyl, Bernstein inequalities) combined with the Meunier et al. (2026) framework, so novelty is concentrated in the augmentation formulation and its consequences rather than new analytic machinery; the improvement over Theorem B.1 of Chen & Christensen (2018) (in-probability vs in-expectation) is real but incremental in scope.

Practical gains in well-aligned regimes (h_old dSprites, small c_alpha synthetic) are modest (~20% improvement) and depend on careful delta tuning, while large delta can clearly degrade performance; the method's robustness to miscalibrated delta is asserted empirically but not theoretically.

strengths: The core operator-theoretic contribution is clean and convincing: Proposition 4.1 establishes that the proposed contrastive loss is exactly a Hilbert–Schmidt best rank-d approximation of the augmented operator Tδ = [T | δr0], giving a principled interpretation of what the outcome-aware regularization is doing rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

The theoretical analysis is more careful than typical for this area: the paper separates a representation-agnostic high-probability 2SLS bound (Theorem 5.1, improving on the in-expectation guarantees of Chen & Christensen 2018) from a perturbation-based approximation analysis (Theorem C.6, Propositions C.3–C.5) that explicitly quantifies when the augmentation fixes spectral misalignment, including the informative 'good'/'bad' scenario comparisons against Meunier et al. (2026). The loss-to-operator-gap bound (Proposition A.4) is a useful standalone technical tool.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations: it states that end-to-end guarantees would require architecture-specific optimization/generalization analysis left open, admits that stage-2 loss selection for δ lacks theoretical justification, and analyzes the instability of the plug-in alignment estimator (∥ω∥→1) in Appendix E.9. This transparency supports reliable interpretation of the results.

The experimental design addresses the failure mode head-on: a new, harder dSprites benchmark (hnew) is constructed with a documented argument (Figure 5, E.1–E.2) for why it exhibits spectral misalignment, and appendix comparisons to naive outcome-aware baselines and rank-K extensions show the authors took alternative designs seriously rather than only comparing against weak strawmen.

Experiments span three regimes (controlled synthetic, image-based semi-synthetic, OPE in RL), and in the misaligned regimes the improvement over SpecIV is large and consistent with the theory's predictions.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are conditional rather than end-to-end: all downstream bounds require a small population optimality gap Ed(θ̂m, ω̂m, δ), and the paper explicitly leaves open the question of whether empirical DNN training achieves this. Thus the theory does not actually establish that the practical estimator is consistent or robust; it characterizes the target the loss should reach.

The choice of δ—a new hyperparameter central to the method—rests on three heuristics, two of which the authors themselves show are problematic: the alignment-based estimator becomes ill-conditioned as δ grows (Appendix E.9), and stage-2 loss selection is admitted to be 'generally unprincipled.' In the OPE experiments δ is tuned as a generic hyperparameter via the very stage-2 loss whose validity is disputed. Practical deployment guidance is therefore weak.

Experimental support is narrower than the framing suggests: the headline misalignment results rely on a benchmark the authors constructed themselves; comparisons are largely limited to DFIV, KIV, and SpecIV, with no minimax/GMM baselines (e.g., AGMM-style methods) in the main NPIV experiments; and OPE results are mixed by the authors' own account (no method performed uniformly well, AugSpecIV and SpecIV 'struggled on Mountain Car'), which tempers the claimed breadth of applicability.

The methodological delta over SpecIV (Sun et al., 2025) is modest: a rank-one augmentation of the operator plus a quadratic penalty term. Much of the machinery (contrastive loss, 2SLS pipeline, spectral analysis framework) is inherited, so the contribution's novelty rests mainly on the perturbation analysis of the augmented operator. Appendix G further shows a simpler two-stage baseline is competitive when its fits are stable, which limits the practical significance of the added machinery.

Reproducibility is compromised: the appendix states the reproduction code 'can be found at .' with the URL missing/blank. Combined with substantial hyperparameter grids (Tables 4–5), an ad hoc 5%-relative-improvement acceptance rule for δ, and a post-hoc rejection rule for the naive baseline, exact replication of the reported figures would be difficult without the code.

Several conditions in the theory are uncheckable in practice (e.g., positivity of the spectral gap γd(δ) in Eq. (8), the signal-to-noise condition ∥s1∥ ≫ λk^{-2}∥q1∥, Eq. (15) requiring κ ≤ 1/2), so the 'bad scenario' guarantee is more of a qualitative explanation than a usable certificate that the method will succeed on a given problem.
